item.content:encoded:
The 39 th Guam Legislature will bring new faces, as well as some returning senators, into Guam’s lawmaking body.

A number of senators in the 38 th Guam Legislature gave up their seats to run for higher office. Republican Speaker Frank Blas Jr., Republican Vice Speaker Tony Ada and Democratic Sens. Therese Terlaje and Joe San Agustin all ran for governor, with Ada winning the island’s highest office.

Democratic Sens. Sabina Perez and Tina Muna Barnes ran for lieutenant governor.

That left nine incumbents, all of whom won reelection.

They are Republicans Sabrina Salas Matanane, Jesse Lujan, Chris Duenas, Shelly Calvo, Telo Taitague, Vincent Borja and Eulogio Shawn Gumatatao. Democratic incumbents reelected were Chris Barnett and William Parkinson.

Former Democratic Sens. Amanda Shelton, Telena Nelson and Clynton Ridgell were elected Tuesday, along with Democratic legislative newcomers Donna Quinata and Kallen Perez.

Hoa Nyugen is the Republican newcomer, giving the party an 8-7 majority in the 39 th Legislature.

item.title: DPHSS to offer free health and social services in Chalan Pago-Ordot
item.description: The Department of Public Health and Social Services will conduct a village outreach program in Chalan Pago-Ordot on Nov. 6. The event runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Chalan Pago-Ordot Multipurpose Emergency Center. Residents can learn about several Public Health programs, get help with applications, and learn about available community resources.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services will conduct a village outreach program in Chalan Pago-Ordot on Nov. 6.

The event runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Chalan Pago-Ordot Multipurpose Emergency Center. Residents can learn about several Public Health programs, get help with applications, and learn about available community resources.

Immunizations will be available for children ages 2 months to 18 years who are enrolled in Medicaid or the Medically Indigent Program or who have no health insurance.

Parents must bring the child’s birth certificate, current immunization record, and their own valid photo ID. Children must be accompanied by a parent or have written authorization or legal documentation allowing another adult to accompany them.

Public Health will also provide educational information on diabetes, tobacco, lead exposure, and hypertension. The Bureau of Child Care Services will have child care assistance applications and program materials available.

Residents can also receive eligibility assessments for the Breast Cervical Cancer Screening Program and the Women, Infants, and Children program. Information will also be available on mental health and primary care services, the aging program, and Adult Protective Services.

Public Health says this is its first village outreach event for fiscal year 2027, part of an effort to make health and social services more accessible to residents.

The department notes that tuberculosis skin tests, also known as PPD tests, will not be offered for the outreach program.

item.title: King-Hinds wins reelection in landslide; Governor, AG races head to runoff
item.description: Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election. item.content:encoded:
Republican incumbent Kimberlyn King-Hinds won reelection Tuesday as the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, capturing nearly two-thirds of the vote in a decisive victory that highlighted the 2026 general election.

Unofficial results showed King-Hinds receiving 8,194 votes, or 63.7% of ballots cast in the delegate race, securing another two-year term in Congress. Independent challenger Galvin Sablan Deleon Guerrero garnered 4,675 votes, or 36%.

While the delegate race produced a clear winner, voters left the contests for governor and attorney general unsettled, triggering runoff elections under CNMI law.

The Republican gubernatorial ticket of Ralph DLG Torres and Benjamin Jones Jr. finished first but failed to capture a majority of votes cast. They will face the independent team of Blas Jonathan Attao and Edmund S. Villagomez in a runoff election.

The independent ticket of Lawrence Camacho and Edith E. Deleon Guerrero finished third and was eliminated from contention.

In the attorney general race, attorneys Joaquin DLG Torres and Michael Evangelista advanced to a runoff after neither candidate secured more than 50% of the vote. Attorney Jonathan Robert Glass Jr. placed third.

The race for attorney general was among the night's closest contests. Evangelista edged Glass by only 18 votes to claim the second runoff spot and keep his campaign alive.

Under CNMI law, a runoff election is required when no gubernatorial ticket or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted in the general election. The runoff must be held within 14 days after the Commonwealth Election Commission certifies the election results.

Voters also considered whether to convene a constitutional convention to propose amendments to the CNMI Constitution. The proposal received majority support, with 7,602 voters casting ballots in favor and 4,324 voting against.

However, the measure failed because it did not meet the constitutional requirement that at least two-thirds of all votes cast on the question commonwealthwide be in favor. As a result, no constitutional convention will be convened.

The results set up two weeks of campaigning before voters return to the polls to decide the governor's office and attorney general post, while King-Hinds prepares to serve another term as the CNMI's representative in Washington.

item.title: It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave

item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.

Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.

In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.

Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.

"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.

"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.

In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)

In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.

Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action , a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.

The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton , says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.

"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.

Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.

Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.

"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."

Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.

During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."

Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.

In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.

Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress .

"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."

In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."

To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.

In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.

In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.

Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."

He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says

Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.

Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys .

"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."

Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.

item.title: Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
item.description: Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99. His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.
item.content:encoded:
Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99.

His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.

In a profession routinely flush with elderly practitioners, Blomstedt, year after year, retained his title as the world's oldest active conductor. He worked into his late 90s, conducting concerts this year, at the age of 98, with the Detroit Symphony and the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, Germany.

"Retirement is not a question of age," Blomstedt told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "It should be flexible. I just love the music so much that I just can't give up." And he didn't.

Blomstedt suffered falls in 2022 and 2023, and an ear infection in 2025, forcing him to cancel performances in Europe and the U.S., but he was undaunted. He resumed adding dates to his schedule, leading the world's top orchestras. In recent years, he conducted while seated at a piano bench. He had plans to conduct a series of concerts with the San Francisco Symphony in May of this year and again in January 2027, both of which were canceled when health concerns got in the way.

"The music-making of elderly conductors can sometimes be either lofty or slow, sometimes both," Martin Kettle wrote in The Guardian in 2022. "Neither quality applies to Blomstedt … his conducting in old age radiates both flow and glow. Blomstedt does not force or underline the music, he releases it. But the attentiveness to pulse, phrasing and dynamics are unflagging."

Blomstedt brought clear-eyed structural integrity and a strict devotion to the composer's score to wide swaths of orchestral music — and eras — from J.S. Bach to Elliott Carter. But late in his career, he distilled his repertoire down to a few favorite Scandinavian composers and a handful of Germanic staples by Bruckner, Brahms, Schubert, Haydn, Mahler and his beloved Beethoven.

He recorded all nine Beethoven symphonies twice, once with the Staatskapelle Dresden, which he led from 1975 to 1985, and later with the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, where he was chief conductor from 1998 to 2005.

"Both cycles remain beacons of good taste, with a distinctive spiritual power shining through," David Allen wrote in The New York Times in 2022. "That's particularly true of the Fifth [symphony], which may be less brutally violent than under other conductors but has a merciful empathy to its relative restraint." Asked by Allen why Beethoven remains such an obsession, Blomstedt pointed to the humanity in the composer's music.

"It can represent the suffering of everyone," Blomstedt answered. "Not only his, but mine. The suffering of today in Ukraine, for instance. That helps it outlive the personal situation of the composer, or the personal situation of the interpreter. It's something that we go through, as humans."

Herbert Thorson Blomstedt was born on July 11, 1927, in Springfield, Mass. to Swedish parents, both Seventh-day Adventist missionaries who returned home when Blomstedt was two, settling in Gothenburg.

In his youth, Blomstedt learned piano, violin and organ, then fell in love with symphonic music. He memorized the names of orchestra players and when the revered German conductor Wilhelm Furtwängler performed in Gothenburg, the shy young Blomstedt asked the maestro for an autograph.

In 1945, Blomstedt entered the Swedish Royal College of Music where he began to study conducting. His education continued with a broad range of influential figures, including stints with John Cage at Darmstadt, Igor Markevitch in Salzburg, Jean Morel at Juilliard and Leonard Bernstein at Tanglewood in 1953, the year in which Blomstedt won the Koussevitzky conducting prize. His formal conducting debut came in 1954 with the Stockholm Philharmonic, moving directly to his first professional post with the Swedish Norrköping Symphony Orchestra.

Blomstedt had close relationships with dozens of orchestras around the world, including the San Francisco Symphony, of which he was music director from 1985 to 1995.

"Blomstedt inherited an orchestra that was skilled and committed but lacking in discipline," says Joshua Kosman, former classical music critic for the San Francisco Chronicle . "Under his guidance, everything became sharper, cleaner, more crisply focused. It was also during his time as music director that the San Francisco Symphony began to tour internationally and record. These two developments were related. Blomstedt made the Symphony, as it were, ready for prime time."

In 2003, Blomstedt returned to lead the Symphony. Kosman said in a review at the time that it only took a few measures of music to realize how much the former music director was missed, especially in a performance of Schumann's Fourth Symphony.

"Looking spry and attentive, Blomstedt led a wonderfully vital performance," he wrote. "And the orchestra — clearly delighted to see its former music director — responded with some of its finest, most spirited playing."

While Blomstedt could elicit ecstatic performances from his orchestras, his own demeanor on the podium was calm and economical with no hint of spotlight-craving showmanship. At times, perhaps too much control led to the occasional indifferent performance. Another return visit to the Symphony in 2013 left Kosman cold. "The program began with the Prelude and "Liebestod" from Wagner's Tristan und Isolde , done with plenty of orchestral richness –- the strings sounded especially robust –- but not much fervor or freedom," he wrote . "Blomstedt is too rational and cautious an interpreter, I think, to make much of this music's luxuriant eroticism."

Blomstedt believed that music could be what he called "an enormous ethical force in society." Speaking with broadcaster Bruce Duffie in 1988, the conductor tried to explain its power. "I'm not so naïve that I think everybody who leaves the concert hall after a Bruckner symphony is saying, 'I won't do so many bad things tomorrow,' but something in that direction," he said. "To experience the order and beauty of great music brings the listener in contact with something greater than himself, something that is meant to be perfect and positive, and this is one of the greatest blessings of great music."

What Blomstedt sensed as something greater than himself was spiritual. A devout Seventh-day Adventist who eschewed alcohol, coffee, tobacco and meat, Blomstedt, early on, refused to rehearse on Saturdays, when he observed the sabbath. It cost him some jobs, he admitted. And yet he conducted concerts on those days, rationalizing that all the real work had been done in rehearsal and performing great music was a spiritual communication to the glory of God.

"I'm a seeker," Blomstedt told journalist Paul Bodine in 2004. "I find God in many places, in nature and scores, in people. I think the ultimate aim of every artist is not to project himself, but there is something in the music that he thinks is important, and when understood by listeners will bring them close to an answer to these eternal questions: Where we come from, why we are here, and where we are going?"

Blomstedt was married to Waltraud Blomstedt, also a Seventh-day Adventist, who held a degree in musicology. She died in 2003 at age 74 in Lucerne, Switzerland, where the couple had lived for years. Blomstedt moved back to Sweden, near Örebro, where three of his four daughters reside.

Earlier this year, the Danish Radio Symphony Orchestra announced plans for Blomstedt to conduct concerts during the three months leading up to his 100th birthday next July.

Always thinking about music and looking ahead, Blomstedt mused, in an interview with Die Welt in the fall of 2025, when he was 98, on what he might conduct for his centennial concerts. Mendelssohn, perhaps, he said. That same year, he told CBS News Sunday Morning , "Without work, I don't live. If I just twiddle my thumbs, that is not living." He said he wanted to be remembered as modest, but truthful and genuine.

"I'm not tired," he said firmly. "Because every time I stand in front of the orchestra, it's like a flame starts to sparkle again. The moment I hear the sound of the orchestra it transforms me."

item.title: Chuck Schumer heralds Democrats' 'generational remake' of Senate
item.description: Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."
item.content:encoded:
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."

"These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," the New York Democrat said outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they — the American people — want."

Democrats secured major gains in red states President Trump has previously carried, including Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Their victories include a history-making win in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years .

Schumer, who is poised to become Senate Majority leader in January, credited these wins to a crop of candidates who "knew how to tailor their message to the states."

Democrats now have a 54-seat majority, including the two independent senators who caucus with the party. Two races have still not been called: Alaska and Mississippi.

Schumer vowed that "relief is on the way" for voters, and acknowledged that some remain skeptical that Democrats will deliver. He said Democrats are intent on bringing down the cost of living, ending the Iran war, and undertaking investigations into the White House to address allegations of corruption.

"The days of Trump's supplicant Senate are over," Schumer declared.

President Trump hasn't shied away from saying he will use his veto pen on Democratic legislative priorities, but has also signaled some openness to cutting deals with the new Democratic-controlled Congress.

"We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him," Schumer said.

item.title: Mike Johnson will step aside as top House Republican next Congress
item.description: Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.
item.content:encoded:
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.

The Louisiana Republican served two terms as speaker, elected after his predecessor, California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023 .

Johnson's decision will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority. Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10.

Historically, the president's party loses seats in midterm elections. The blue wave soared past the expectations of many in Washington, flipping seats in traditionally red states that the president has won previously.

Johnson nodded to that history in remarks Tuesday night.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history. It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle. There's a lot of reasons for it. It's very, very difficult to overcome, and it looks like history will be kept tonight," he said.

Johnson worked closely with the Trump administration throughout his tenure as speaker, and endured the balancing act of trying to keep his conference united with the narrowest of majorities. His razor thin majority meant even one Republican defection meant GOP priorities were at risk.

That dynamic will not be replicated for the presumptive next House Speaker, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York. While there are a handful of lawmakers elected with support of the Democratic Socialists of America , eager to push the party further to the left, the comfortable margin for Jeffries means he will likely be able to achieve his priorities, even with defections.

His speakership would be history making — he would be the first Black lawmaker elected to the position .
